children.html: Online interpersonal sexual objectification experiences and Chinese adolescent girls' intuitive eating: The role of broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation
Yi-jun Luoa,b,c , Geng-feng Niud , Fan-chang Kongc , Hong Chena,b,⁎
• a Key Laboratory of Cognition and Personality (Ministry of Education), Southwest University, Chongqing 400715, China
• b School of Psychology, Southwest University, Chongqing 400715, China

Keywords: Online interpersonal sexual objectification experiences Intuitive eating Broad conceptualization of beauty Body appreciation Adolescent girls

Interpersonal sexual objectification experiences are pervasive in online communication contexts, and their influence on positive eating behaviors should not be ignored. Broad conceptualization of beauty refers to how widely women and girls define female beauty in terms of both internal and external characteristics, and body appreciation refers to loving, respecting, and holding a positive attitude toward the body. This study examined the association between online interpersonal sexual objectification (OISO) experiences and intuitive eating, as well as the mediating role of broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation. Participants were 1152 Chinese adolescent girls aged 11 to 15 years who completed a questionnaire survey measuring OISO experiences, broad conceptualization of beauty, body appreciation, and intuitive eating. The results showed a negative association of OISO experiences with broad conceptualization of beauty and intuitive eating. Mediation analysis using structural equation modeling showed a negative association of OISO experiences with intuitive eating through broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation. These results suggest that programs aiming to improve healthy eating behaviors could direct adolescent girls to criticize the appearance-focused mindset in online interaction and encourage them to focus on body functionality, such as health, creative endeavors, and communication with others.

In the field of eating behaviors, scholars have focused largely on how to prevent eating disorder symptomatology (Jackson & Chen, 2014; Walker et al., 2015). However, the absence of pathology does not necessarily imply positive eating behaviors (Tylka & Wilcox, 2006). Therefore, it has been noted that research must also examine positive eating behaviors that foster and maintain overall psychological health (Tylka, 2006), such as intuitive eating. Intuitive eating refers to a strong trust in and connection with internal, physiological hunger and satiety cues guiding what, when, and how much to eat (Tylka, 2006). Studies have reported strong associations between intuitive eating and female psychological and physical health outcomes, such as self-esteem (Schoenefeld & Webb, 2013), internal body orientation (Tylka & Homan, 2015), glycemic control for type I diabetes mellitus (Wheeler et al., 2016), and positive treatment outcomes for eating disorder patients (Richards, Crowton, Berrett, Smith, & Passmore, 2017).
Therefore, investigating the predictors of intuitive eating not only helps develop healthy eating habits, but could contribute to psychological and physical health outcomes as well.

Conceptually, sexual objectification theory posits that women and girls who experience sexual objectification from interpersonal sources are more likely to exhibit restrictive eating behaviors because their objectification experiences guide them to adopt an observer's perspective on their external appearance, emphasize their external appearance rather than their inner characteristics, and consequently restrict themselves from certain foods (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). In the current information society, social media has increased in popularity over the last decade. A total of 93.6% of middle school students in China use social media (China Internet Network Information Center, 2016), and 71% of teens in the USA report using social media platforms (Pew Research Center, 2015). Given that adolescent girls constantly communicate with friends online, it is important to consider that interpersonal sexual objectification experiences, such as objectifying

evaluations of the body and emphasis on appearance, are ubiquitous in online communication contexts. For example, women and girls regularly receive appearance-related feedback from peers on social media (Kim & Chock, 2015; Vries, Peter, Graaf, & Nikken, 2015), and their selfies are tagged by peers so that every friend on social media is able to see them (Meier & Gray, 2014). Sometimes, women and girls receive requests to send selfies because others are highly interested in how they look. These experiences create the impression that others focus more on external female appearance than inner beauty. Objectifying evaluations of body parts and emphasis on appearance are found to be the main aspects of interpersonal sexual objectification (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997; Kozee, Tylka, Augustus-Horvath, & Denchik, 2007). Accordingly, in the present study, we define online interpersonal sexual objectification (OISO) experiences as experiences that suggest others are paying extensive attention to external appearance in an online context, such as "someone evaluates your size or appearance in your photo album" or "you receive requests from someone to post your photo". Conceptually, the more OISO women and girls experience, the less they may engage in intuitive eating, because those who constantly encounter OISO may pay considerable attention to their body shape and further monitor what they eat to control their weight. Empirically, direct evidence has found that female college students who are highly objectified are more likely to focus on external appearance and have fewer available resources to attend to internal hunger, and therefore eat less intuitively (Andrew, Tiggemann, & Clark, 2015). Indirect evidence has found that young women are easily engaged in fat talk in online contexts, which is positively associated with disordered eating behaviors (Walker et al., 2015). Adolescent girls who frequently feel appearance pressure—for example, being included in a friend's photos—report higher levels of body image disturbance (Meier & Gray, 2014). A China-based longitudinal study shows that objectified body consciousness can predict disordered eating at one-year follow-up for college students (Jackson & Chen, 2015). Because disordered eating is negatively related to intuitive eating for both adolescents and adults (Linardon & Mitchell, 2017; Moy, Petrie, Dockendorff, Greenleaf, & Martin, 2013), it has been suggested that OISO experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating. A previous study examining the relationship of sexual objectification and intuitive eating measured self-objectification but not experiences of sexual objectification (Andrew et al., 2015). To address this gap, the present study seeks to investigate the relationship between OISO experiences and intuitive eating, which could help apply objectification theory to the online context. Building on the previous research, we hypothesize that OISO experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating.

The acceptance model of intuitive eating demonstrates that broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation contribute to development of intuitive eating (Andrew, Tiggemann, & Clark, 2016). Broad conceptualization of beauty is defined as the extent to which women and girls widely define female beauty in terms of both internal and external characteristics (Tylka & Iannantuono, 2016); women and girls with a broad conceptualization of beauty perceive a wide range of appearances and sizes as beautiful and tend to focus more on confidence and self-acceptance (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Body appreciation is defined as loving and respecting the body, appreciating the body's functions, rejecting societal ideals of attractiveness, feeling comfortable with the body, focusing on the body's assets rather than imperfections, and processing body-related information positively rather than negatively (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a; Wood-Barcalow, Tylka, & Augustus-Horvath, 2010). In the present study, broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation were expected to play a mediating role in the association between OISO experiences and intuitive eating. A series of studies demonstrate that sexual objectification guides women and girls to internalize the thin-ideal as their beauty standard (Calogero, Pina, Park, & Rahemtulla, 2010; Kozee et al., 2007). It is suggested that those women and girls who encounter sexual objectification would accept socioculturally idealized images and

embrace external beauty as their beauty standard. In this way, they would also care less about their personality and possess a narrower conceptualization of beauty (Fardouly, Willburger, & Vartanian, 2018). OISO experiences would thus be negatively associated with broad conceptualization of beauty.

Drawing on objectification theory (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997), OISO experiences are considered to be negatively associated with body appreciation, because they guide girls to prioritize size and appearance over inner characteristics. Empirical study has shown a positive association between everyday body evaluation and body shame (Carr & Szymanski, 2011). Additionally, body evaluation and unwanted sexual advances are related not only to body shame, but to more serious trauma symptoms (Miles-McLean et al., 2015). Interpersonal sexual objectification also predicts social motives for cosmetic surgery through increased body shame (Calogero et al., 2010). The above research suggests that OISO experiences should be negatively associated with body appreciation. Furthermore, girls with higher body appreciation have been found less likely to eat when emotionally distressed (Annesi & Mareno, 2015) or to restrict their consumption of food they want (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005). In other words, the more often girls encounter OISO, the more they may believe that beauty is based on external appearance and aligned with sociocultural ideals. Thus, they may pay more attention to their own appearance and engage in less intuitive eating behaviors. A longitudinal study found that body appreciation increases intuitive eating (Andrew et al., 2016), suggesting that girls who have a positive attitude toward and love for their bodies are aware of when, what, and how much to eat, and are inclined to respect their bodies and eat based on inner hunger cues (Avalos & Tylka, 2006). Broad conceptualization of beauty has been found to be positively related to body appreciation (Bailey, Gammage, van Ingen, & Ditor, 2015; McHugh, Coppola, & Sabiston, 2014). Women and girls who perceive beauty based on inner characteristics tend to respect their bodies and resist sociocultural beauty standards, and thus have a higher level of body appreciation. Therefore, we hypothesize that OISO experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating through decreased levels of broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation.

Because girls' eating attitudes and behaviors develop in adolescence (Graber, Brooks-Gunn, Paikoff, & Warren, 1994), investigation of intuitive eating among adolescent girls could provide implications for both positive eating behaviors and eating pathology. However, previous studies applying objectification theory to the acceptance model of intuitive eating ignore sexual objectification experiences in the online context (Andrew et al., 2016), and evidence from non-Western samples is still lacking. To address these gaps, the present study seeks to investigate whether OISO experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating, as well as the role of broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation in this association. A serial mediation model based on the above evidence is proposed.

After ethics approval was received from Southwest University, Chongqing, potential settings were contacted, and all permitted the study. A pencil-and-paper survey was conducted including 1250 Chinese adolescents girls between 11 and 15 years of age. Participants were recruited from four public schools in Wuhan City, Hubei province. Data collection took approximately 2 months. Before completing the pencil-and-paper survey, adolescents and their legal parent/guardian provided informed consent. Participants were informed that the purpose of the study was to investigate their online behaviors, body image, and eating behaviors; that their answers would be analyzed only by the principal investigators; and that they could withdraw their participation at any time. All participants completed the questionnaire designed

to collect information on age, weight, height, time spent on QQ (the most widely used social media platform in China, on which users may communicate instantly, post text, photo, or video updates, be tagged by anyone, and comment on the same screens), OISO experiences, broad conceptualization of beauty, body appreciation, and intuitive eating. The scales were translated into Chinese by a student with a master's degree, then back into English by a student with a doctorate (both of whom majored in English) to ensure that the original item meanings were preserved. Following the survey, every participant received a pencil for their participation. A total of 1152 questionnaires were included in the present analysis.
Participants reported their current height (meters) and weight (kilograms). Participants' BMI was calculated according to the following formula: weight (kilograms)/(height [meters])2 .
Participants reported their time (hours) spent on QQ on a regular day.

OISO experiences were measured using six items. Two were derived from an item from the Interpersonal Sexual Objectification Scale (Kozee et al., 2007): the original item, "How often have you felt like or known that someone was evaluating your physical appearance?", was changed to "How often have you noticed someone evaluating your size or appearance in your photo album on Q-zone?" and "How often have you noticed someone evaluating your size or appearance during QQ communication?". The remaining four items were added based on QQ features, the most typical adolescent QQ behaviors reported by China Internet Network Information Center (2016), and the concept of interpersonal sexual objectification. Two doctoral psychology students who studied online behaviors and body image were involved in development of the items (see Appendix). Participants indicated the frequency with which they encountered OISO experiences on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Cronbach's α was 0.82. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was performed. The significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity, χ2 (15) = 2687.32, p < .001, and the size of the Kaiser-Meyer-Oklin measure of sampling adequacy, KMO = 0.74, demonstrated adequate common variance of the six items for factor analysis (Tabachnick & Fidell, 1996). EFA yielded a single factor accounting for 52.49% of the total variance. All six items had factor loadings higher than 0.48. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed to assess the single-factor model, and the model was found to adequately fit the data, RMSEA = 0.072, χ2 (6) = 6.82, CFI = 0.987, TLI = 0.967, SRMR = 0.021.

The Broad Conceptualization of Beauty Scale (Tylka & Iannantuono, 2016) was used to measure broad conceptualization of beauty. Participants indicated their agreement with statements (e.g., "Even if a physical feature is not considered attractive by others or by society, I think that it can be beautiful") on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 5 (completely agree). Cronbach's α was 0.81. CFA was performed to assess the 9-item single factor model, and the model adequately fit the data, RMSEA = 0.072, χ2 (24) = 6.79, CFI = 0.954, TLI = 0.932, SRMR = 0.039.

The Body Appreciation Scale-2 (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b) was used to measure body appreciation. Participants indicated their agreement with statements (e.g., "I respect my body") on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 5 (completely agree). Cronbach's α

was 0.89 for the present sample. CFA was performed to assess the 10 item single factor model, and the model adequately fit the data, RMSEA = 0.078, χ2 (24) = 7.72, CFI = 0.967, TLI = 0.937, SRMR = 0.030.

The four-factor intuitive eating scale for adolescents (Dockendorff, Petrie, Greenleaf, & Martin, 2012) was used to measure intuitive eating. Participants indicated their agreement with statements (e.g., "I can tell when I'm slightly full") on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 5 (completely agree). Cronbach′ α was 0.70 for Unconditional permission to eat, 0.81 for Eating for physical rather than emotional reasons, 0.81 for Trust in internal hunger/satiety cues, and 0.73 for Awareness of internal hunger/satiety cues. The overall Cronbach's α for intuitive eating was 0.75. CFA was performed to assess the four-factor model. Item 17 was not loaded on any of the four factors, and therefore only 16 items were used in the analysis. The model adequately fit the data, RMSEA = 0.057, χ2 (110) = 5.13, CFI = 0.935, TLI = 0.919, SRMR = 0.054.

Prior to analysis, missing data imputation (2.2%) was conducted using HotDeck Imputation (Myers, 2011). Mean, standard deviation, and correlation were computed using SPSS version 18. To assess the proposed model, variance-adjusted weighted least squares (WLSMV) estimation was conducted using Mplus version 7. The significance of the indirect effect was calculated using Sobel's test (Sobel, 1982). For the WLSMV method, cutoff values close to 0.95 for TLI and CFI, close to 0.06 for RMSEA, and close to 1.00 for WRMR can be considered good fit indices (DiStefano, Liu, Jiang, & Shi, 2018; Hu & Bentler, 1999). To assess the fit of the model, χ2 , degrees of freedom (df), TLI, CFI, RMSEA, and WRMR were calculated (Muthén & Muthén, 2012).

Means, standard deviations, and bicorrelations for all study variables are presented in Table 1. OISO experiences were negatively associated with broad conceptualization of beauty and intuitive eating. Broad conceptualization of beauty, body appreciation, and intuitive eating were positively correlated. However, OISO experiences were not associated with body appreciation.

First, the psychological variables were represented as latent variables indicated by the multiple items from their questionnaire measures. Second, model fit was examined after controlling for age, BMI, and time spent on QQ. Model fit data are presented in Table 2. The proposed model demonstrated good fit across multiple criteria. One path, OISO experiences to body appreciation, was not significant. To obtain a more parsimonious model, the path was deleted and the model was reexamined. The trimmed model provided a better fit to the data (see Table 2). Chi-square difference testing for WLSMV showed that the trimmed model did not differ from the original model. Therefore, the trimmed model was retained. Standardized parameter estimates for the structural relations in the proposed model are shown in Fig. 1. Third, we examined whether broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation mediated the relationship between OISO experiences and intuitive eating. In support of our hypothesis, broad conceptualization of beauty partially mediated the relationship between OISO experiences and intuitive eating (indirect effect β = −0.066, SE = 0.028, p < .05). This study is the first to explore factors influencing intuitive eating among Chinese adolescent girls. The results show an indirect effect of OISO experiences on intuitive eating through broad conceptualization of beauty, and an indirect effect of OISO experiences on intuitive eating through broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation. Overall, the study adds to the body of research demonstrating that sexual objectification experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating, and it broadens the application of objectification theory and the acceptance model of intuitive eating.

Our findings suggest that girls who encounter OISO more often are more likely to value their external body shape, care less about their internal body experiences, and eat less intuitively. This finding aligns with previous evidence that browsing and posting selfies on social media is associated with increased body shame (Meier & Gray, 2014). Social media have become increasingly popular among adolescent girls, increasing the potential for girls to encounter sexual objectification. Programs intended to improve healthy eating behaviors could direct adolescent girls to critique the appearance-focused mindset of online interaction and encourage them to focus on body functionality (what their body is capable of). For example, the Body Project, which guides girls in critiquing the media-portrayed thin-ideal, for example by asking them to list the benefits and costs of being thin, has been shown to effectively reduce body dissatisfaction and disordered eating in adolescent girls (Stice, Shaw, Burton, & Wade, 2006). The Expand Your Horizon program, which trains women to pay greater attention to body functionality, can improve body satisfaction and reduce self-objectification (Alleva, Martijn, Van Breukelen, Jansen, & Karos, 2015). Future intervention programs could be developed using the OISO experience items to assist adolescent girls in critiquing interpersonal objectifying contents online. Additionally, intervention programs could concentrate on guiding adolescent girls away from focus on appearance and instead
to value body functions such as health, creative endeavors, and communication with others.

Our findings also show that girls with higher OISO experience scores are less likely to accept a wide range of appearances and sizes as beautiful. This finding is consistent with that of a prior study, which demonstrates that interpersonal sexual objectification influences women to internalize the sociocultural thin-ideal as their desired body shape and to adopt a positive attitude toward cosmetic surgery (Calogero et al., 2010). The present results also show that girls with broader conceptualizations of beauty report higher levels of intuitive eating. This suggests that girls who think of female beauty differently from its portrayal in the media, and who perceive a wide range of body sizes as beautiful, are more likely to eat based on their inner cues rather than emotional reasons. A previous study has similarly shown that women with a broad conceptualization of female beauty have lesser anti-fat attitudes and greater appreciation for their body shape (Tylka & Iannantuono, 2016). Furthermore, the present study shows that broad conceptualization of beauty mediates the relationship between OISO experiences and intuitive eating, implying that broadening girls' conceptualization of beauty is critical. School-based programs should thus develop lesson plans illustrating the conceptualization of beauty from a perspective of diversity, compassion, and acceptance (Tylka & Iannantuono, 2016). In addition, parents and peers should express more appreciation for the bodies of their daughters and their friends so as to broaden the conceptualization of beauty and increase intuitive eating.

Our findings indicate that girls who love and respect their bodies report higher levels of intuitive eating. This is in line with the acceptance model of intuitive eating (Augustus-Horvath & Tylka, 2011; Avalos & Tylka, 2006), demonstrating that the model is applicable for Chinese girls. However, the findings do not show an association of OISO experiences with body appreciation, demonstrating that although OISO experiences present the idea that external appearance is of high importance, they are unable to threaten participants' positive body image. Similar results are presented by a recent longitudinal study investigating the predictors of body appreciation, which shows that consumption of appearance media (e.g., Facebook) does not predict a decreased level of body appreciation (Andrew et al., 2016). The present findings highlight that positive body image may be relatively stable, and could be utilized by adolescent girls to resist the negative influence

of interpersonal sexual objectification experiences. Furthermore, because OISO experiences are negatively associated with intuitive eating through broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation in the present study, broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation could act as buffers, protecting adolescent girls from the negative impact of OISO experiences and to some extent guaranteeing their ability to eat intuitively.

The findings from this study provide several contributions to the existing research. First, this study extends prior research by shedding light on a new form of interpersonal sexual objectification among adolescent girls, and by revealing its negative relationship with intuitive eating. The study highlights that interpersonal sexual objectification can occur in online environments, and that girls who experience OISO frequently exhibit less intuitive eating behaviors. It should be noted that the OISO experiences scale was developed for the present study based on a Chinese social media platform (QQ), which may hinder generalization or replication of the study results. However, the experiences that are described in each item can apply to other forms of social media. For example, item 1, "How often have you noticed someone evaluating your size or appearance in your photo album on Qzone?", could be used in the Facebook context by changing "photo album on Q-zone" to "selfies on Facebook." To date, evaluation of others' appearance has been pervasive among Facebook users (Kim & Chock, 2015).

Second, this study explores factors associated with intuitive eating, drawing on objectification theory and the acceptance model of intuitive eating, based on a relatively large sample of Chinese adolescent girls. The findings support and extend the application of these two theories. A previous longitudinal study has shown that Chinese adolescent girls who perceive pressure from peers to be thin may in turn develop disordered eating habits (Jackson & Chen, 2014). However, given that intuitive eating is not solely defined by the absence of disordered eating
symptoms (Tylka & Wilcox, 2006), this study is the first to explore factors associated with intuitive eating in Chinese adolescent girls.

Third, this study emphasizes the mediating role of broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation between OISO experiences and intuitive eating. Our results provide a new perspective for intervention programs aiming to foster positive eating behaviors — that is, to reject the message OISO experiences suggest to adolescent girls, to broaden girls' conceptualization of beauty, and to increase girls' body appreciation.

Despite the above contributions, the study has several limitations. First, the study is cross-sectional; therefore, it cannot establish casual relationships. Future studies should employ longitudinal or experimental designs to make inferences regarding causality. Additionally, the OISO experiences scale was developed for the present study based on a specific Chinese social media platform, which limits the generalizability of the results. Future studies based on other social media should adapt the scale to suit the specific context.

The online context, in which most adolescent girls engage daily, presents the impression that others focus most on girls' external appearance. Unfortunately, the present study finds such experiences to be negatively associated with intuitive eating. However, because broad conceptualization of beauty and body appreciation are positively associated with intuitive eating, broadening conceptualization of beauty and increasing body appreciation in future intervention programs may help to facilitate positive eating behaviors.
